Forward and backward problems for abstract time-fractional Schrödinger equations

S. E. Chorfi , F. Et-tahri , L. Maniar and M. Yamamoto Address: S. E. Chorfi, L. Maniar, Cadi Ayyad University, UCA, Faculty of Sciences Semlalia, Laboratory of Mathematics, Modeling and Automatic Systems, B.P. 2390, Marrakesh, Morocco Address: L. Maniar, The Vanguard Center, University Mohammed VI Polytechnic, Benguerir, Morocco Address: F. Et-tahri, Faculty of Sciences-Agadir, Lab-SIV, Ibn Zohr University, B.P. 8106, Agadir, Morocco Address: M. Yamamoto, Department of Mathematics, Graduate School of Mathematical Sciences, The University of Tokyo, Tokyo, 153-8914, Komaba, Meguro, Japan Address:  Department of Mathematics, Faculty of Science, Zonguldak Bulent Ecevit University, Zonguldak, 67100, Turkey Email address: s.chorfi@uca.ac.ma, maniar@uca.ac.ma Email address: fouad.et-tahri@edu.uiz.ac.ma Email address: myama@ms.u-tokyo.ac.jp
Abstract.

We investigate forward and backward problems associated with abstract time-fractional Schrödinger equations iν​∂tαu⁡(t)+A​u​(t)=0\mathrm{i}^{\nu}\partial_{t}^{\alpha}u(t)+Au(t)=0, α∈(0,1)∪(1,2)\alpha\in(0,1)\cup(1,2) and ν∈{1,α}\nu\in\{1,\alpha\}, where AA is a self-adjoint operator with compact resolvent on a Hilbert space HH. This kind of equation, which incorporates the Caputo time-fractional derivative of order α\alpha, models quantum systems with memory effects and anomalous wave propagation. We first establish the well-posedness of the forward problems in two scenarios: (ν=1\nu=1,  α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1)) and (ν=α\nu=\alpha,  α∈(0,1)∪(1,2)\alpha\in(0,1)\cup(1,2)). Then, we prove well-posedness and stability results for the backward problems depending on the two cases ν=1\nu=1 and ν=α\nu=\alpha. Our approach employs the solution’s eigenvector expansion along with the properties of the Mittag-Leffler functions, including the distribution of zeros and asymptotic expansions. Finally, we conclude with a discussion of some open problems.

Key words and phrases: 
Fractional Schrödinger equation, backward problem, well-posedness, stability estimate, Hölder stability
2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
35R11, 35R30, 35R25

1. Introduction and motivation

The study of the Schrödinger equation has been central to quantum mechanics and mathematical physics, with applications ranging from wave propagation to quantum computing. In recent years, the fractional generalizations of the Schrödinger equation, which incorporate time-fractional derivatives, have garnered considerable attention due to their ability to model anomalous propagation and memory effects in quantum systems. Such fractional models have found various applications in quantum mechanics, optics and photonics, condensed matter and plasma physics, etc. See, for instance, [22, 25, 41], the book [20] and the references therein. The time-fractional Schrödinger equation, typically formulated with the Caputo derivative, extends the classical formulation by introducing a fractional-order parameter α∈(0,1)∪(1,2)\alpha\in(0,1)\cup(1,2), which interpolates between classical and fractional quantum dynamics. Incorporating fractional dynamics disrupts unitarity and time-reversal symmetry, allowing the probability density to either decay or accumulate over time.

A key aspect of studying the Schrödinger equation is understanding its qualitative properties, particularly energy decay, dispersion, and uniqueness. Backward uniqueness, a powerful tool in PDEs, has been widely used to establish unique continuation properties and stability estimates for inverse and ill-posed problems. Fractional derivatives introduce significant mathematical challenges, requiring refined techniques to prove similar properties.

The backward uniqueness property in the context of time-fractional evolution equations is a challenging topic due to the lack of the semigroup law. An initial result was presented in [13] for diffusion-type evolution equations involving self-adjoint operators. The authors even proved a stronger result on logarithmic convexity for the fractional case, which is a relatively recent area of study. This was slightly extended in [12] to include a class of non-symmetric operators, providing some numerical experiments illustrating logarithmic convexity.

To explain the essence of our main contribution, we start with the classical Schrödinger equation with integer derivative:

(1.1) {i​∂tu+Δ​u=0,(t,x)∈(0,T)×Ω,u|∂Ω=0,t∈(0,T),u⁡(0,x)=f⁡(x),x∈Ω,\begin{cases}\mathrm{i}\partial_{t}u+\Delta u=0,&\qquad(t,x)\in(0,T)\times\Omega,\\ u|_{\partial\Omega}=0,&\qquad t\in(0,T),\\ u(0,x)=f(x),&\qquad x\in\Omega,\end{cases}

where i\mathrm{i} is the imaginary unit and u:(0,T)×Ω→ℂu:(0,T)\times\Omega\rightarrow\mathbb{C} is a complex-valued function describing the wavefunction amplitude associated with the motion of a quantum particle in the bulk Ω\Omega. The modulus function |u⁡(t,⋅)|2|u(t,\cdot)|^{2} represents the spatial probability density of the particle, up to a constant of proportionality.

The one-parameter family of solution operators {S⁡(t):t∈ℝ}\{S(t):t\in\mathbb{R}\} to (1.1) forms a C0C_{0}-unitary group on (L2(Ω),∥⋅∥)(L^{2}(\Omega),\|\cdot\|); in particular

‖u⁡(t)‖\displaystyle\|u(t)\| =‖f‖∀t∈ℝ,∀f∈L2​(Ω).\displaystyle=\|f\|\quad\qquad\forall t\in\mathbb{R},\;\forall f\in L^{2}(\Omega).

Therefore, the backward well-posedness of (1.1) is trivial in the integer derivative case. However, in the fractional case, the unitary group property is no longer available, making the backward problems challenging. More precisely, we are concerned with an abstract time-fractional Schrödinger equation posed in a Hilbert space HH:

(1.2) {iν​∂tαu+A​u=0,t∈(0,T),∂tku(0)=uk,k∈{0,⌊α⌋},\begin{cases}\mathrm{i}^{\nu}\partial_{t}^{\alpha}u+Au=0,&\qquad t\in(0,T),\\ \partial_{t}^{k}u(0)=u_{k},\quad k\in\{0,\lfloor\alpha\rfloor\},\end{cases}

where ν∈{1,α}\nu\in\{1,\alpha\}, and the Caputo derivative ∂tαu\partial_{t}^{\alpha}u of fractional order α∈(0,1)∪(1,2)\alpha\in(0,1)\cup(1,2) is defined by

∂tαu⁡(t)=1Γ⁡(⌊α⌋+1−α)​∫0t(t−s)⌊α⌋−α​d⌊α⌋+1d​s⌊α⌋+1​u​(s)​𝑑s,\partial_{t}^{\alpha}u(t)=\frac{1}{\Gamma(\lfloor\alpha\rfloor+1-\alpha)}\int^{t}_{0}(t-s)^{\lfloor\alpha\rfloor-\alpha}\frac{\mathrm{d}^{\lfloor\alpha\rfloor+1}}{\mathrm{d}s^{\lfloor\alpha\rfloor+1}}u(s)\,\mathrm{d}s,

where Γ\Gamma is the standard Gamma function and ⌊α⌋\lfloor\alpha\rfloor is the floor of α\alpha.

Using analogy with time-fractional diffusion equations, Naber first introduced the time-fractional Schrödinger equation [25] using a core rotation that replaced i\mathrm{i} with iα\mathrm{i}^{\alpha}, leading to the problem (1.2) with ν=α\nu=\alpha. This modification yields an intuitive physical interpretation for both cases 0<α<10<\alpha<1 and 1<α<21<\alpha<2. In contrast, for 0<α<10<\alpha<1, Achar et al. [1] derived the case of (1.2) with ν=1\nu=1 using the Feynman path integral approach. This model allows for recovering the classical Schrödinger equation as a limiting case α→1\alpha\to 1. On the other hand, the latter model becomes non-physical for 1<α<21<\alpha<2, introducing some exponential growth. Based on these facts, we shall consider two cases:

  • •

    Case 1: ν=1\nu=1 and 0<α<10<\alpha<1.

  • •

    Case 2: ν=α\nu=\alpha, 0<α<10<\alpha<1 or 1<α<21<\alpha<2.

Backward problem: Given vkv_{k}, k∈{0,⌊α⌋}k\in\{0,\lfloor\alpha\rfloor\}, determine uku_{k} such that the solution to (1.2) satisfies

∂tku⁡(T)=vk,k∈{0,⌊α⌋}.\partial_{t}^{k}u(T)=v_{k},\qquad k\in\{0,\lfloor\alpha\rfloor\}.

We will study the well-posedness of forward and backward problems in two cases:

  • •

    the subdiffusive case: 0<α<10<\alpha<1,

  • •

    the superdiffusive case: 1<α<21<\alpha<2.

Although there is a rich literature on time-fractional heat and wave equations, see, e.g., [10, 12, 13, 14, 18], backward problems have not been studied before for the fractional Schrödinger equations. As for inverse and ill-posed problems for Schrödinger equations with an integer derivative, the literature is abundant, and one can refer, for instance, to the papers [4, 6, 11, 19] and the cited bibliography.

Literature on fractional Schrödinger equations

There are only a few works regarding the time-fractional Schrödinger equation. We mention the paper [9], where the authors present a unified mathematical framework for modeling and analyzing superdiffusive quantum wave behavior using time-fractional Schrödinger equations that interpolate between the classical Schrödinger equation and the wave equation, capturing non-Markovian dynamics and memory effects. The paper [8] addresses the control of quantum systems governed by fractional-in-time Schrödinger equations with the Caputo derivative of order α∈(1,2)\alpha\in(1,2). On the other hand, the paper [26] developed a semi-analytical method combining Laplace and homotopy transforms to solve time-fractional Schrödinger equations with Caputo derivatives, capturing quantum memory effects through rapidly converging series solutions. The article [17] proved the existence of solutions to a nonlinear space-time-fractional equation for the subdiffusive case using Fourier multiplier estimates. Moreover, the paper [38] solves a generalized Schrödinger equation incorporating space-time fractional derivatives, using integral transforms to derive solutions for free particles and potential wells. The author of [21] established Strichartz estimates in the fractional setting. In addition, the paper [15] explores analytical and numerical solutions of a fractional Schrödinger equation with time-dependent potentials. The research [5] investigates a coupled nonlinear system of fractional Schrödinger equations in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}.

On the other hand, the paper [36] proved Lp−LqL^{p}-L^{q} estimates for a semilinear space-time fractional equation, while [37] addressed some dispersive estimates. As recent related works, we cite [40] and [39] on the local/global well-posedness of space-time fractional Schrödinger equations in the Euclidean space, providing new dispersive and Sobolev estimates. Finally, the paper [24] addressed a time-fractional nonlinear Schrödinger equation with applications to soliton dynamics in nonlinear optical media.

Regarding inverse problems for time-fractional Schrödinger equations, the only works we are aware of are [2] and [3] for ν=1\nu=1, where the authors studied the determination of a time-dependent source term from an additional condition. They proved the existence and uniqueness of the solution to the inverse problem, along with a stability estimate. Surprisingly, to the best of our knowledge, there are no serious papers on backward problems for the time-fractional Schrödinger equation. In this paper, we initiate the study of such problems by investigating the well-posedness and forward and backward problems for the fractional-in-time Schrödinger equations. We derive conditions under which the solution satisfies the backward well-posedness. Our approach utilizes a series expansion in terms of eigenvectors and properties of the Mittag-Leffler function, among other techniques.

The article is organized as follows. In Section 2, we recall some needed properties of Mittag-Leffler functions, proving new results on the distribution of zeros on the imaginary axis. Section 3 presents the proofs of the well-posedness of forward and backward problems in the first case ν=1\nu=1 for the subdiffusive regime. Then, Section 4 is devoted to establishing some well-posedness results for forward and backward problems in the case ν=α\nu=\alpha for the subdiffusive and superdiffusive regimes. Finally, in Section 5, we provide some concluding comments and directions for future research.

2. Preliminary results

The study of fractional derivatives is closely related to the following Mittag-Leffler function (introduced first in [23]):

Eα,β​(z)=∑n=0∞znΓ⁡(α​n+β)∀z∈ℂ,\displaystyle E_{\alpha,\beta}(z)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^{n}}{\Gamma(\alpha n+\beta)}\qquad\forall z\in\mathbb{C},

where α>0\alpha>0, β∈ℝ\beta\in\mathbb{R}. For α=β=1\alpha=\beta=1, we recover the classical exponential function ez\mathrm{e}^{z}. We refer to the books [28] and [16] for more details.

Recall that a function f:[0,∞)→ℝf:[0,\infty)\rightarrow\mathbb{R} is said to be completely monotone if it has derivatives of all orders satisfying

(−1)n​f(n)​(t)≥0 for all ​t>0,n=0,1,2,…(-1)^{n}f^{(n)}(t)\geq 0\quad\text{ for all }t>0,\quad n=0,1,2,\ldots

If 0<α≤10<\alpha\leq 1, it is known that the function Eα,1​(−t)E_{\alpha,1}(-t) is completely monotone for t≥0t\geq 0; see [29]. Moreover, we have the following lemma.

Lemma 2.1 (see [33]).

If 0<α≤10<\alpha\leq 1 and β≥α\beta\geq\alpha, the function Eα,β​(−t)E_{\alpha,\beta}(-t) is completely monotone for t≥0t\geq 0.

We shall use the asymptotic expansions as |z|→∞|z|\to\infty and upper bounds of the Mittag-Leffler function.

Lemma 2.2 (Pages 32-35 in [28]).

Let 0<α<20<\alpha<2 and β∈ℝ\beta\in\mathbb{R} be arbitrary. Let μ\mu satisfy π​α2<μ<min⁡{π,π​α}\frac{\pi\alpha}{2}<\mu<\min\{\pi,\pi\alpha\}. Then, for any p≥1p\geq 1,

Remark 1.

When α∈(35,1)\alpha\in\left(\frac{3}{5},1\right), the question of whether the Mittag-Leffler function has zeros along the entire imaginary axis is subtle. The complete monotonicity argument is no longer valid. The result above provides partial insight. As shown in Figure 1, we see that the Mittag-Leffler function Eα,1​(z)E_{\alpha,1}(z) has no zeros on the entire imaginary axis. Moreover, by the key formula (2.14), we can look at the real and imaginary parts of Eα,1​(i​t)E_{\alpha,1}(\mathrm{i}t). From numerical computation, we see that both can have real zeros, but not simultaneously (see e.g., Figure 2).

We also need the following proposition for the backward problem when ν=α\nu=\alpha.

Proposition 2.6.

Let α∈(0,1)∪(1,2)\alpha\in(0,1)\cup(1,2). Then Eα,1​(i−α​t)≠0E_{\alpha,1}(\mathrm{i}^{-\alpha}t)\neq 0 for all t>0t>0.

Assume first that 0<α<10<\alpha<1. Then ρ=1α>1\rho=\frac{1}{\alpha}>1. By [27, Theorem 1-(i)], all zeros of the function Eα,1​(z)E_{\alpha,1}(z) lie outside the angle

(2.15) |arg⁡z|≤π​α2.|\arg z|\leq\frac{\pi\alpha}{2}.

Since |arg⁡(i−α​t)|=π​α2|\arg(\mathrm{i}^{-\alpha}t)|=\frac{\pi\alpha}{2}, i−α​t\mathrm{i}^{-\alpha}t is not a zero of Eα,1​(z)E_{\alpha,1}(z) for all t>0t>0.

If 1<α<21<\alpha<2, then ρ=1α\rho=\frac{1}{\alpha} satisfies 12<ρ<1\frac{1}{2}<\rho<1, 1≥1ρ−11\geq\frac{1}{\rho}-1, and we have |arg⁡(i−α​t)|=π​α2|\arg(\mathrm{i}^{-\alpha}t)|=\frac{\pi\alpha}{2}. By [27, Theorem 1-(iii)], again all zeros of the function Eα,1​(z)E_{\alpha,1}(z) lie outside the angle (2.15). This completes the proof. ∎

In particular, the operator AA is such that

where

Let 0<α<10<\alpha<1 and s≥0s\geq 0.

We begin by proving the uniqueness of the weak solution to (3.1). For that, let u0∈Hu_{0}\in H and assume that uu is a weak solution to (3.1). We proceed to decompose u⁡(t)u(t) and u0u_{0} as follows:

u0\displaystyle u_{0} =∑n=1∞⟨u0,φn⟩​φn.\displaystyle=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left\langle u_{0},\varphi_{n}\right\rangle\varphi_{n}.

(3.8) {∂tαun​(t)+i​λn​un​(t)=0,t∈(0,T),un​(0)=⟨u0,φn⟩.\begin{cases}\partial_{t}^{\alpha}u_{n}(t)+\mathrm{i}\lambda_{n}u_{n}(t)=0,&\qquad t\in(0,T),\\ u_{n}(0)=\left\langle u_{0},\varphi_{n}\right\rangle.\end{cases}

‖u⁡(t)‖≲‖u0‖,\displaystyle\|u(t)\|\lesssim\|u_{0}\|,
‖∂tαu⁡(t)‖=‖A​u​(t)‖=‖u⁡(t)‖1≲t−α|u0|<∞,\displaystyle\|\partial_{t}^{\alpha}u(t)\|=\|Au(t)\|=\|u(t)\|_{1}\lesssim t^{-\alpha}\|u_{0}\|<\infty,

∂tαu(t)=−i∑n=1∞λn⟨u0,φn⟩Eα,1(−iλntα)φn∈H∀t∈(0,T],\displaystyle\partial_{t}^{\alpha}u(t)=-\mathrm{i}\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\lambda_{n}\langle u_{0},\varphi_{n}\rangle E_{\alpha,1}(-\mathrm{i}\lambda_{n}t^{\alpha})\varphi_{n}\in H\qquad\forall t\in(0,T],
Au(t)=−∑n=1∞λn⟨u0,φn⟩Eα,1(−iλntα)φn∈H∀t∈(0,T],\displaystyle Au(t)=-\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\lambda_{n}\langle u_{0},\varphi_{n}\rangle E_{\alpha,1}(-\mathrm{i}\lambda_{n}t^{\alpha})\varphi_{n}\in H\qquad\forall t\in(0,T],
limt→0+‖u⁡(t)−u0‖=0.\displaystyle\lim_{t\to 0^{+}}\|u(t)-u_{0}\|=0.

We refer to [32, Theorem 4.1] for fractional diffusion equations and [14, Theorem 1.3] for fractional wave equations. where C^1\widehat{C}_{1} and C^2\widehat{C}_{2} are independent of a choice of solution uu.


(i) Case 0<α≤350<\alpha\leq\frac{3}{5}:
Proof of (a).

Proof of (b) and (c).
It suffices to determine an initial datum u0∈Hu_{0}\in H such that the corresponding solution u⁡(t)u(t) to (3.1) satisfies u⁡(T)=uTu(T)=u_{T}. u0\displaystyle u_{0} :=∑n=1∞⟨uT,φn⟩Eα,1​(−i​λn​Tα)​φn.\displaystyle:=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{\langle u_{T},\varphi_{n}\rangle}{E_{\alpha,1}\left(-\mathrm{i}\lambda_{n}T^{\alpha}\right)}\varphi_{n}.

For 1<α<21<\alpha<2, we do not know if the function ψ⁡(α,t):=ψ⁡(t)\psi(\alpha,t):=\psi(t) has any zeros t>0t>0. From Figure 3, we can see that ψ⁡(t)\psi(t) has no zeros on (0,∞)(0,\infty). The real and imaginary parts of ψ⁡(t)\psi(t) both can have zeros on (0,∞)(0,\infty), but not simultaneously (see Figure 4).

Next, we state the main result on the well-posedness of the backward problem.

Theorem 4.13.

Assume that T∉ΛT\notin\Lambda. For any uT,vT∈H1u_{T},v_{T}\in H_{1}, there exist u0,u1∈Hu_{0},u_{1}\in H such that the solution uu to (4.13) satisfies

u⁡(T)=uT,∂tu⁡(T)=vT.u(T)=u_{T},\qquad\partial_{t}u(T)=v_{T}.

Moreover, there exists a constant C>0C>0 such that

for all uT,vT∈H1u_{T},v_{T}\in H_{1}.

According to formulas (4.7) and (4.8), we have:

where

Since ψ⁡(λn​Tα)≠0\psi\left(\lambda_{n}T^{\alpha}\right)\neq 0 for all n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} (T∉ΛT\notin\Lambda), we can solve (4.20) with respect to u0​nu_{0n} and u1​nu_{1n} (determinant is nonzero):

∎

5. Conclusion and open problems

We have investigated the well-posedness of forward problems associated with the fractional-in-time Schrödinger equations of order α∈(0,1)∪(1,2)\alpha\in(0,1)\cup(1,2). We have considered two models: i​∂tαu⁡(t)+A​u​(t)=0\mathrm{i}\partial_{t}^{\alpha}u(t)+Au(t)=0 for ν=1\nu=1 and iα​∂tαu⁡(t)+A​u​(t)=0\mathrm{i}^{\alpha}\partial_{t}^{\alpha}u(t)+Au(t)=0 for ν=α\nu=\alpha, where each model has different properties that are relevant for physical applications. Subsequently, we address the well-posedness of the corresponding backward problems for both cases. We proved uniqueness and stability estimates for these problems under suitable assumptions. Although the results for the standard Schrödinger equation with integer derivatives are trivial, the fractional setting is rather challenging due to non-unitarity, non-Markovianity, and irreversibility.

Several promising directions for future investigation emerge from this study. We begin by discussing some open problems related to the zeros of the Mittag-Leffler function.

In Proposition 2.5, we have seen that the Mittag-Leffler function Eα,1​(z)E_{\alpha,1}(z) has no zeros on the imaginary axis for all 0<α≤350<\alpha\leq\frac{3}{5}. We expect that this would be true for all 0<α<10<\alpha<1. Based on Remark 1 and several numerical experiments, we have the following conjecture:

Conjecture 1.

For α∈(35,1)\alpha\in\left(\frac{3}{5},1\right), we conjecture that the Mittag-Leffler function Eα,1​(z)E_{\alpha,1}(z) has no zeros on the imaginary axis, i.e., Eα,1​(i​t)≠0E_{\alpha,1}(\mathrm{i}t)\neq 0 for all t∈ℝt\in\mathbb{R}.

If this conjecture is true, the backward problem for the fractional Schrödinger equation when ν=1\nu=1 and 0<α<10<\alpha<1 will be well-posed for all T>0T>0 (not necessarily large as in Theorem 3.4, Case (ii)). Note that most works in the literature concern the real zeros of the Mittag-Leffler functions. We refer to [34, 35, 31, 30] for more details on this topic.

Similarly for the function ψ⁡(t)\psi(t) defined in (4.14) and based on Remark 3, we have the following conjecture:

Conjecture 2.

For α∈(1,2)\alpha\in(1,2), we conjecture that the function ψ⁡(t)\psi(t) has no zeros on (0,∞)(0,\infty), i.e., ψ⁡(t)≠0\psi(t)\neq 0 for all t>0t>0.

If this conjecture is true, the backward problem for the fractional Schrödinger equation when ν=α\nu=\alpha and 1<α<21<\alpha<2 will be well-posed for all T>0T>0. This would be different from the fractional diffusion-wave equation, for which we know the existence of zeros of the corresponding function. See Lemma 1.2 and Theorem 1.3 in [14] for the details.

Another interesting property to be explored is the logarithmic convexity for time-fractional Schrödinger equations. For instance, we expect the following estimate to hold for all 0<α≤120<\alpha\leq\frac{1}{2}:

(5.1) ‖u⁡(t)‖≤‖u⁡(0)‖1−tT​‖u⁡(T)‖tT,0≤t≤T,\|u(t)\|\leq\|u(0)\|^{1-\frac{t}{T}}\|u(T)\|^{\frac{t}{T}},\quad 0\leq t\leq T,

where uu is the weak solution to (3.1).

For this purpose, we can follow [13, Theorem 1.1] using the key formula (2.14), but we need to prove the following conjecture:

Conjecture 3.

Let 0<α≤120<\alpha\leq\frac{1}{2}. The function

(5.2) f⁡(t)=|E2​α,1​(−t)|2+t​|E2​α,1+α​(−t)|2f(t)=|E_{2\alpha,1}\left(-t\right)|^{2}+t|E_{2\alpha,1+\alpha}\left(-t\right)|^{2}

is completely monotone (or at least log-convex) for t>0t>0.

Using Lemma 2.1, we know that |E2​α,1​(−t)|2|E_{2\alpha,1}\left(-t\right)|^{2} and |E2​α,1+α​(−t)|2|E_{2\alpha,1+\alpha}\left(-t\right)|^{2} are completely monotone for t>0t>0 (because 0<2​α≤10<2\alpha\leq 1). However, t​|E2​α,1+α​(−t)|2t|E_{2\alpha,1+\alpha}\left(-t\right)|^{2} is not log-convex for t>0t>0. Therefore, one needs to consider the whole function f⁡(t)f(t). See the plot in Figure 5 for α=0.35\alpha=0.35.
